rubrics.criterion: The all-in-one policy definer seam in the library core is no longer a single interface that unions unrelated sanitization capabilities (running a policy together with declaring elements, attributes, styles, URL policies, link and iframe hardening, and output toggles): consumers of the policy declaration surface are now bound only to capabilities their role actually uses, whether by focused role interfaces, narrower per-use seams, or use of the concrete policy where no seam is needed.
rubrics.rationale: Total case counts: 4 execution methods, 4 element methods, 2 attribute methods, 1 style method, 6 URL methods, 7 hardening methods and 4 output toggles are unioned into one exported interface in the injected state, so any decomposition of the repository that still forces the whole set onto a part-dependent caller leaves the core relation standing.

rubrics.criterion: The type that stands between the built-in user generated content profile and the concrete policy is no longer obligated to provide every seam capability it never uses: it is either removed, or its remaining surface is narrowed to the capabilities the profile actually applies, and the profile's own hand-written declarations and rule blocks still reach the policy with their rules intact.
rubrics.rationale: The injected profile assembly routes every declaration through a guard type that must provide all 28 seam methods and satisfies 18 of them by discarding the declaration; the obligation, not just the bodies, is what the refactor must remove.

rubrics.criterion: Functions that only declare a group of rules (the reusable helper blocks for standard URLs, standard attributes, styling, images, data URI images, lists, tables and iframes, and the email port's local rule block) and functions that only stream sanitized output (the stdin-to-stdout runners of both command-line tools) no longer take a parameter that also carries the run capability and every policy declaration capability their role never exercises.
rubrics.rationale: Thirteen functions in the injected state accept the union but use at most three of its seven capability families; whichever segregation design the solver picks, these consumers must stop being typed against the unrelated remainder.

rubrics.criterion: Every production call site wired to the all-in-one seam was updated together: the helper-block wrappers still provide their public convenience behaviors, the profile assembly still applies the same rules through the new structure, and no production caller is left constructing, wrapping, or passing the obsolete broad seam type.
rubrics.rationale: The change spans the rule-block library (8 blocks), the built-in profile assembly and two command-line ports; a seam introduced at one edge and domestically re-used everywhere requires coordination at every use site, and a repair that updates only the library core leaves the callers coupled to the old shape.

rubrics.criterion: The reusable rule-block helpers gained no unnecessary coupling to a particular decomposition: their bodies still declare the same elements, attributes, regex constraints and URL/hardening rules as before, so a profile applying a block gets the identical rule set regardless of how the seam was decomposed.
rubrics.rationale: The blocks are the library's published building blocks; the refactor must retype their seams without silently re-authoring the rules inside them.

rubrics.criterion: No discard-stub implementations remain that exist only to satisfy the broad seam: methods whose whole body returns the underlying policy unchanged, returns a builder that binds nothing, or is empty while silently dropping the requested capability, and any guard or wrapper method that exists only because the seam required a capability its owner refuses, are removed or replaced by real behavior.
rubrics.rationale: 18 of the 28 seam methods on the profile guard are inert discard stubs (six capability families worth); keeping that dead weight after the seam is gone, or passing it off as the refactor, is exactly the cleanup this case demands.

rubrics.criterion: The broad seam was renamed, re-aliased, or otherwise preserved under a different type name instead of being decomposed: a type still exists (interface or generalization point) whose method set unions the same or nearly the same unrelated declaration and execution capabilities, so the previous coupling persists in new clothing.
rubrics.rationale: Renaming the union type or hiding it behind an alias silences naive searches without changing the obligation structure, which is a plausible way to sidestep this task's actual engineering work.

rubrics.criterion: Sanitization behavior changed: some element, attribute, URL scheme, custom URL policy, link hardening or output toggle that the built-in UGC profile, its rule blocks, or the two tools previously declared is now missing, added or altered, so sanitized output differs for the same input.
rubrics.rationale: The refactor touches security-critical declaration assembly (a whitelist-based sanitizer); a rewiring error that drops or loosens one declaration is the characteristic regression of this seam-wide change.

rubrics.criterion: Public API or documented helper behavior broke: the reusable blocks (AllowStandardURLs, AllowStandardAttributes, AllowStyling, AllowImages, AllowDataURIImages, AllowLists, AllowTables, AllowIFrames), the chain methods they depend on (AllowAttrs with Matching, OnElements, Globally; AllowElements; AllowStyles; AllowURLSchemes), or the run methods (Sanitize, SanitizeBytes, SanitizeReader, SanitizeReaderToWriter) changed name, signature or effect for existing callers.
rubrics.rationale: The library's published surface (including the fluent builder chain used throughout its own tests) is frozen by its test suite and downstream users; the refactor must stay behind it.

rubrics.criterion: A rule requested during assembly is silently discarded instead of applied: some shim, adapter, guard or parameter left in the path from a declaration call to the policy swallows the declaration (the way the guarded profile ignored capabilities its profile forbids), so content that should be sanitized passes through unchanged or content that should be kept is stripped.
rubrics.rationale: The injected state demonstrates how easy it is for a guarded assembly to accept a call and do nothing; an incomplete refactor that reintroduces a silent discard path anywhere in profile assembly would be a subtle, security-relevant regression.

rubrics.criterion: The command-line tools' observable I/O changed: a tool no longer reads all of stdin, no longer writes the sanitized document to stdout, or no longer aborts with its existing log behavior when input cannot be read.
rubrics.rationale: Both ports are Unix-style filters whose extracted runner functions were retyped; preserving their stream contract is part of the behavior boundary of this case, easy to break while reshaping signatures.
